What the app does with your data

No analytics, ads, trackers or accounts. The ShrimpNG developers get nothing about you: the project runs no servers the app would report to. Below is every case where the app goes online by itself, and everything it has access to.

No usage statistics, crash reports, advertising IDs, or third-party SDKs that would send them. There are no Google services or Firebase in the app either. Which servers and sites you use is never sent anywhere.

The app fetches a subscription link from whoever issued it — manually, or on a schedule if you turned on auto-update. The request goes through the VPN, or directly if it isn't connected. The subscription server sees:
• the User-Agent “ShrimpNG/version” (or your own, if the subscription sets one);
• by default, a device ID (HWID), the phone model and the Android version. The HWID is the Android ID the system issues to this app specifically; other apps see a different one. Panels like Remnawave use it to limit devices.
To turn the HWID off or use your own: App settings → “Send device ID (HWID)”.

The ping method is chosen in app settings:\n• HTTP through the server (default) — the client opens www.gstatic.com/generate_204 (Google) through the server being tested. Google sees the server\'s address, not yours. The app also does this on its own after connecting with some profiles, to find a TLS fingerprint that works.\n• TCP and TLS — the app connects to the server itself directly, so it sees your IP, as with any connection.

With the VPN on, names of sites that go through the proxy are resolved with Cloudflare (1.1.1.1), also through the proxy.\nNames of sites in “direct” rules are resolved with Yandex DNS (77.88.8.8) by default — outside the VPN, so your ISP and Yandex see those lookups. Both are changed in the DNS settings.

• Once a day, rule files (geosite, geoip) from GitHub, through the VPN if it is connected. Turned off on the Asset files screen.\n• The app list for per-app proxy — from GitHub, only when you tap import.\nGitHub sees the IP the request came from and nothing else: no device ID is added to these requests.

• VPN — to route traffic through the server you chose.
• Camera — only to scan QR codes. Frames are not saved or sent anywhere.
• Location — only for the “Trusted Wi-Fi” rule: without it Android won't tell apps the network name. Neither your location nor the network name is sent anywhere. If you don't use the rule, it isn't requested.
• App list — so you can choose which apps use the VPN. Stays on the device.
• Clipboard — read only when you paste a key or open “Add” on the home screen.
• Notifications — connection status and speed.

Servers, keys, subscriptions, rules and settings are kept only in the app's own storage.
• Connection history: the last 50 — time, length, server, subscription, address and that session's log at the chosen level. The level, and turning it off, are on the Logs screen. Behind the calculator disguise no history is kept and it is wiped on auto-lock. At the Debug level the connection config, keys included, goes into the log.
• The firewall journal is off by default. When on, it records which app connected to which address and keeps that for 3 days. To show names instead of IPs it makes reverse DNS lookups outside the VPN, which your ISP sees.
• Logs leave the device only if you share them. Backups go to a file or to your WebDAV — only when you ask.
One caveat: Android's system backup is enabled for the app. If backup to your Google account is on, the app's data, keys included, may end up in your Google Drive backup.
The website, the Telegram chat and channel (where “Check for updates” leads, too) and GitHub open only when you tap them — in your browser or in Telegram, under their own rules.
